title: Where Did Your $100 Go? 54 Years of Inflation, Explained with Data
description: In 1970, a hundred-dollar bill bought what you need about $808 for today. Where did the rest go? With 54 years of official US price data, we take inflation apart: what it measures, why it compounds, the shocks of 1980 and 2022, how other countries compare – and who quietly wins and loses when money loses value.
sources: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Consumer price index (2010 = 100), FP.CPI.TOTL – United States, 1970–2024 (CC BY 4.0)
World Bank, World Development Indicators: Inflation, consumer prices (annual %), FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG – United States, Switzerland, Japan, Germany, United Kingdom, Brazil, Nigeria, Türkiye (CC BY 4.0)
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Consumer Price Index – how the CPI is calculated (bls.gov/cpi)
Federal Reserve Board: Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy (January 2012) – the 2 percent inflation goal

beats.say: Here's a hundred-dollar bill from 1970. Same paper, same green, same face on the front.
But if you wanted to buy today what that bill bought back then, you'd need about eight hundred and eight dollars.
Or, turned around: a hundred dollars today buys roughly what twelve dollars bought in 1970.
Nobody stole it. It didn't vanish in one big crash. It leaked away, a few percent a year, for fifty-four years.

show.caption: what today's $100 was worth in 1970 money

beats.say: So let's take that leak apart, piece by piece, with the official price data – and see where your hundred dollars actually went.
First, what are we even measuring? Inflation is not the price of one thing. It's the price of a whole shopping basket.

show.text: *Inflation* = how much more the same basket of goods and services costs than a year before.
show.source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI

beats.say: In the United States, the Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks the prices of thousands of items every month: food, rent, fuel, clothes, doctor visits, phone plans.
Each item gets a weight, depending on how much of their money households really spend on it. Rent counts a lot. Postage stamps, very little.
Put it all together and you get one number: the consumer price index. When it rises by three percent in a year, the typical basket costs three percent more.
That's all inflation is. Not one price going up, but the value of each dollar going down, measured against everything it can buy.
Now let's take that index and draw it, year by year, from 1970 to 2024. To keep it simple, we start the line at one hundred dollars.
Watch the shape. It never really goes down. It just climbs – slowly in some decades, steeply in others.
By 1980, the basket that cost a hundred dollars already cost about two hundred and twelve. By 2000, four hundred and forty. And by 2024, about eight hundred and eight.
Spread over fifty-four years, that's an average of just under four percent a year. Four percent sounds harmless. Fifty-four years of it multiplies prices by eight.
And that's the trick of inflation: every year it looks small. It's the stacking that makes it big.
Why does a small number stack up so fast? Because inflation compounds. Each year's increase is added on top of last year's higher prices.
Here's a quick way to feel it. It's called the rule of seventy-two: divide seventy-two by the yearly rate, and you get roughly how many years it takes for prices to double.
At two percent a year, prices double in about thirty-six years. At four percent, in about eighteen. At eight percent, in only nine.
Here's what that does over the same fifty-four years. Start with a hundred dollars of prices and let them grow at two, four and eight percent a year.

show.heading: $100 of prices after 54 years
show.sub: Compound growth at a fixed yearly rate

beats.say: At two percent, the hundred dollars becomes about two hundred and ninety. At four percent – close to the American path – about eight hundred and thirty.
And at eight percent, it ends above six thousand three hundred dollars. Same fifty-four years, just a few more points a year.
And that's almost exactly what happened. At just under four percent, US prices doubled about every eighteen years: three doublings in fifty-four years. Two, four, eight.
The rule works the other way round, too. Money that just sits there loses half its buying power in the same number of years.
But the average hides the drama. Let's draw the yearly inflation rate instead – how much prices rose in each single year.
The first big spike: 1974, above eleven percent, after an oil shock pushed energy prices up across the economy.
Then the peak: 1980, thirteen and a half percent. At that pace, prices would double in just over five years.
It took very high interest rates in the early 1980s to bring it down. By 1983, inflation was close to three percent again.
Then came decades of calm. In 2009, after the financial crisis, prices even fell slightly for a year – minus zero point four percent.
And then 2022: eight percent, the highest since 1981. Supply chains, energy, and a lot of spending after the pandemic all pushed in the same direction.
By 2024 it had cooled to about three percent. But notice what didn't happen: prices didn't go back down. Lower inflation means prices rise more slowly – not that they fall.
Is four percent a year normal? It depends a lot on where you live. Here's the average yearly inflation from 2014 to 2024 in eight countries.
Switzerland: about half a percent. Japan: just over one. Germany, the US and Britain: between two and three.
Brazil: close to six. Nigeria: over sixteen. And Turkey: around twenty-six percent a year on average.
At twenty-six percent, the rule of seventy-two says prices double in under three years. Planning anything – a salary, a rent contract, a savings goal – becomes a guessing game.

show.caption: to double prices at 26% a year

beats.say: That's why stable prices are so valuable. Not because low inflation is exciting, but because it lets people plan.
So who actually loses when money loses value? First, cash that just sits still. A hundred dollars under a mattress in 1970 is still a hundred dollars – it just buys an eighth as much.
The same goes for anything paid in fixed dollars: a pension that isn't adjusted for inflation, or a salary that doesn't rise, shrinks a little every year.
And who gains? Anyone who owes a fixed amount. A loan with a fixed rate is repaid in dollars that are worth less each year, so the debt gets lighter in real terms.

show.text: Inflation shrinks what money is worth – *including the money you owe.*
show.source: This is how inflation works, not a tip on what to do.

beats.say: That's why economists talk about real values: the number on the bill, adjusted for what it can buy. A raise of three percent when prices rise three percent is a raise of zero.
If inflation eats money, why don't central banks aim for zero? The Federal Reserve, for example, officially targets two percent a year, and has since 2012.

show.caption: the Federal Reserve's inflation goal since 2012

beats.say: Part of the reason is a safety margin. When prices fall across the board – deflation – people and companies tend to wait, spend less, and debts become heavier.
Japan lived through exactly that. Between 1995 and 2020, its consumer prices rose by about four percent in total – not per year, in twenty-five years.
In fifteen of the thirty-five years since 1990, prices actually fell. Many companies held wages flat, and the economy grew only slowly for years.

A small, steady, predictable rise in prices is easier to live with than either extreme. The problem is never two percent. It's the surprises: the thirteen percent years, and the ones nobody planned for.
So where did your hundred dollars go? Nowhere dramatic. It leaked away a few percent at a time, and the leak compounded for fifty-four years.

show.caption: 1970 buying power, measured in today's dollars

beats.say: Three things to remember: inflation is the price of a whole basket. Small yearly rates double prices faster than they feel. And what matters is never the number on the bill – it's what the bill can buy.
If this made money a little less mysterious, subscribe – next time we'll take apart another piece of the economy, with real numbers.
Here's a hundred dollars from 1970. To buy the same shopping today, you'd need about eight hundred and eight dollars.
Turned around, today's hundred dollars buys what about twelve dollars bought back then.
Here's the line: official US consumer prices, from 1970 to 2024. It never really goes down. It just climbs.
The average was just under four percent a year. Sounds small. But inflation compounds, and the rule of seventy-two tells you how fast: seventy-two divided by four is eighteen.
So prices doubled about every eighteen years. Three doublings in fifty-four years: two, four, eight.
The worst single year was 1980, at thirteen and a half percent. The latest spike was 2022, at eight.
Nobody stole your money. It just leaked, a few percent a year. How much did your money lose since you were born? Tell me in the comments.
